Grantham
GRAN-thum
n. (the Lincolnshire town whose dispute of 1627 over moving the communion table altarwise produced the classic Reformed English defence of the holy table)
Old English probably Granta ham, the homestead on the Granta or gravelly stream; a Lincolnshire market town on the Witham.

Definition · Webster 1828 · Scriptures · Corruption · Roots · Usage · Related

Biblical Definition

Grantham is the Lincolnshire market town on the Witham, with a parish church whose spire is among the tallest in England and a grammar school where Isaac Newton was a pupil. Its place in the dictionary is a parish quarrel that became a national argument. In 1627 the vicar, Peter Titley, moved the communion table from the body of the chancel, where it had stood table-wise since the Reformation with the people gathered round it, and set it altarwise against the east wall; the alderman and the townsmen objected and the matter went to the bishop of Lincoln, John Williams. Williams ruled for the townsmen, and in 1637 published his judgment and its grounds as The Holy Table, Name and Thing, arguing that the Church of England had deliberately replaced an altar with a table because it had replaced a sacrifice with a supper, and that to move the furniture back was to reintroduce by stealth the thing the Articles denied. Laud had him prosecuted in Star Chamber and imprisoned in the Tower. The dictionary records the case as the clearest English statement that furniture teaches doctrine.

Webster 1828 Definition

Webster (1828) defines an altar as a place for sacrifice; a table as a board for meals; a supper as the evening meal; decently as in a becoming manner; and a tradition as a practice handed down.

expand to see more

ALTAR, n. A mount, table or elevated place, on which sacrifices were anciently offered to some deity.

TABLE, n. An article of furniture consisting of a flat surface supported by legs; the table of the Lord's supper.

SUPPER, n. The evening meal; the last meal of the day; the Lord's supper, the sacrament of the eucharist.

DECENTLY, adv. In a decent or becoming manner; with propriety of behaviour; without immodesty.

TRADITION, n. The delivery of opinions, doctrines, practices or rites from father to son by oral communication.

Key Scripture

Joh 4:24 — "God is a Spirit: and they that worship him must worship him in spirit and in truth."

1Co 14:40 — "Let all things be done decently and in order."

Mat 15:9 — "But in vain they do worship me, teaching for doctrines the commandments of men."

Col 2:23 — "Which things have indeed a shew of wisdom in will worship, and humility, and neglecting of the body; not in any honour to the satisfying of the flesh."

Modern Corruption

Lincolnshire town whose vicar moved the communion table altarwise in 1627, against which Bishop John Williams ruled for the townsmen and published The Holy Table, Name and Thing in 1637, for which Laud imprisoned him.

expand to see more

The corruption to name is the restoration of the altar, and the dictionary names it as doctrine carried by carpentry. The Reformers had taken down stone altars and set up wooden tables in the body of the chancel because an altar implies a sacrifice and a priest who offers it, while a table implies a meal and guests who receive it; the change was deliberate and was the visible form of the Articles' denial that the mass is a propitiatory sacrifice. To push the table back against the east wall, rail it in and bow toward it was to teach the old doctrine again without having to argue it, which is why Williams fought over a few feet of chancel. Our Lord's rule removes the question from the realm of fittings altogether: “God is a Spirit: and they that worship him must worship him in spirit and in truth” (Joh 4:24).

The second paragraph grants the Laudian case its one real point and then answers it. Order in worship is commanded, and Paul closes his treatment of a disorderly church with the rule, “Let all things be done decently and in order” (1Co 14:40); a parish where the table is set anywhere and treated anyhow is not thereby more spiritual. But order is not the same as ceremony, and an arrangement introduced by authority without warrant from Scripture falls under the Lord's own condemnation of worship that rests on human command: “in vain they do worship me, teaching for doctrines the commandments of men” (Mat 15:9). Paul describes the whole class of such observances as impressive and empty, having “a shew of wisdom in will worship” (Col 2:23). The dictionary adds that Williams was no Puritan, being a prelate who defended his own order; that he was imprisoned in the Tower for publishing a defence of the English Reformation's own settled practice is the measure of how far the Laudian party had travelled.

Greek & Hebrew Roots

Greek pneuma (G4151), spirit; Greek taxis (G5010), order; Greek ethelothreskeia (G1479), will worship.

expand to see more

Greek pneuma (G4151) — breath, spirit; “God is a Spirit”, John 4:24.

Greek aletheia (G225) — truth, reality; “must worship him in spirit and in truth”, John 4:24.

Greek taxis (G5010) — an arranging, order, a fixed succession; “Let all things be done decently and in order”, 1 Corinthians 14:40.

Greek entalma (G1778) — an injunction, a commandment of men; “teaching for doctrines the commandments of men”, Matthew 15:9.

Greek ethelothreskeia (G1479) — self-chosen worship; “a shew of wisdom in will worship”, Colossians 2:23.

Usage

"“must worship him in spirit and in truth” (Joh 4:24) — the question removed from the realm of fittings."

"“Let all things be done decently and in order” (1Co 14:40) — the Laudian case at its strongest."

"“teaching for doctrines the commandments of men” (Mat 15:9) — a table railed in and bowed toward."
